panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A shows a patient biopsy with H&E evidence of a subepidermal blister, consistent with the article's diagnosis of pseudoporphyria. B: Panel B shows a patient biopsy with H&E evidence of a subepidermal blister and caterpillar bodies, supporting pseudoporphyria.

panels.figure_caption: Hematoxylin-eosin staining of punch biopsy taken from left medial shin (10× magnification) showing a subepidermal blister. A, The cavity contains mononuclear cells and granulocytes—mainly neutrophils but also eosinophils. B, The blister roof comprises epidermis showing degenerative features and there are “caterpillar bodies” adherent to the undersurface of the epidermis (arrow). (A and B, Hematoxylin-eosin stain; original magnification: 10×.)
in_text_mentions: Results of the punch biopsy (Fig 2A, B) were consistent with a subepidermal bullous disorder, showing a subepidermal blister with sparse mononuclear cells and granulocytes, in addition to “caterpillar bodies” adherent to the undersurface of the epidermis. in_text_mentions: led inflammatory poor sub-epidermal vesicular dermatitis. Further immunofluorescence revealed a linear deposit of C3 at the dermo-epidermal interface, as well as the absence of immunoglobulin (IG) A, IGG, IGM, and C1Q (Figure 2). The serum antinuclear antibody (ANA) profile was within normal ranges in blood testing. Clinical and histological evidence led to the diagnosis of pseudoporphyria. The woman was given topical corticosteroids and 600 mg of N-acetylcysteine orally daily for a month, but no improvement was seen in her skin condition, and new lesions continued to emerge all over her body.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of the patient's pinna showing crusted erosions and scarring, matching the caption and the in-text description of blisters rupturing into erosions that heal with scarring in a case of drug-induced (NSAID) pseudoporphyria. Ear/pinna is a sun-exposed but less commonly illustrated site, hence variant typicality. Skin tone assessed as medium from visible, adequately lit skin; age and ethnicity not stated in the caption or text.
panels.attribution_text: Jangid et al. Drug-Induced Pseudoporphyria: A Case Report.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.57574. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Erosions and scars over the pinna.

These fluid-filled lesions would burst spontaneously over two to three days to form erosions (Figure 3), which would heal with scarring over two to three months. The lesions were associated with increased burning during sun exposure. panels.rationale: Real patient clinical photograph from a case report of drug-induced pseudoporphyria showing healed-phase disease on sun-exposed facial skin: post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation with irregular scarring, matching the caption and the described scar-forming blistering history. Pigmentation/scarring is a recognized sequela rather than the active bullae, hence variant typicality.

panels.figure_caption: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation with multiple irregular scars.
in_text_mentions: A 20-year-old male patient presented to our dermatology outpatient department with the chief complaints of multiple erosions with irregular scars on the face (Figure 1) and dorsum of bilateral hands (Figure 2) for one year. He gave a history of fluid-filled lesions over the same site, which were associated with itching and burning. These fluid-filled lesions would burst spontaneously over two to three days to form erosions (Figure 3), which would heal with scarring over two to three months. panels.rationale: The image is a clinical photograph of a human patient presenting with pseudoporphyric lesions over the anterior abdominal wall. The caption explicitly states these are 'Pseudoporphyric lesions' and the in-text mentions describe 'erythematous skin lesions... with fluid-filled vesicles and bullae', which are consistent with the included finding.

in_text_mentions: Following the hemodialysis, the patient acquired erythematous skin lesions all over the body with fluid-filled vesicles and bullae with cutaneous fragility (Figure 1), for which dermatological consultation was sought and assessed. After a thorough examination and ruling out other potential causes of porphyria (the porphyrin profile was within normal limits), a biopsy of the lesion revealed inflammatory poor sub-epidermal vesicular dermatitis.
